text.title: Checkpoint Ledger Failure Modes
text.summary: Six ways an on-disk ledger fails. Four have been observed in production runs of this orchestrator; each carries the rule that closes it.

failure.symptom: A unit appears in the queue that nobody enrolled. It sits at phase zero, and the dispatcher offers to run work that was already partly done under the correct id.
failure.cause: The marker tool created its own state directory, so a mistyped unit id produced a second directory instead of an error.
failure.prevention: One creation path. Every other writer verifies the directory exists and exits non-zero when it does not. Observed here: a mistyped slug produced a phantom unit whose only symptom was an offer to redo four of seven completed phases.

failure.symptom: A phase shows no marker at all after a crash or a kill. Nobody can tell whether it was dispatched, so recovery is a coin flip between redoing paid work and skipping unfinished work.
failure.cause: The marker was written when the agent returned. An agent that never returns writes nothing.
failure.prevention: Write the marker first. A crash then leaves a stuck marker with a timestamp — a positive signal the sweep can act on instead of an absence it has to interpret.

failure.symptom: After an incident, nobody can reconstruct the order of events. The state directory shows where each unit is and nothing about how it got there.
failure.cause: Only current-status markers were kept; each transition overwrote its predecessor.
failure.prevention: One append-only line per transition, under a lock. Markers are derived and disposable; the log is the record and is never rewritten, including by rollback.

failure.symptom: A phase is re-run repeatedly and keeps producing output that is internally consistent and wrong. Three-strikes escalation fires and the operator has nothing to act on.
failure.cause: The only recovery verb was retry. A phase that succeeded and produced a bad artefact had no path back, because downstream phases had already consumed it.
failure.prevention: Add rollback as a separate verb: truncate markers at and after the phase in lineage order, record `rolled-back` with a reason, requeue there with an amended brief.

failure.symptom: Two agents write the same output file. Cost for the phase doubles and the artefact is a mixture of two runs.
failure.cause: A staleness timer re-dispatched an `in-flight` phase without checking whether the original agent was still alive. Long-running phases tripped the timer legitimately.
failure.prevention: Check liveness before acting, set the threshold against the longest phase rather than the average, and route to dead-letter rather than re-dispatch. Observed here on translation units that routinely run past 150 minutes.

failure.symptom: After an outage the orchestrator resumes everything at once and hits the rate limit within minutes, leaving a second wave of stale markers behind it.
failure.cause: Automatic crash-resume ran ahead of the gate that normally throttles dispatch, and every resumed dispatch was full-price uncached input.
failure.prevention: Resume is an operator decision routed through the same gate as a first dispatch. Prompt caching is hardcoded off for subagent dispatches (`anthropics/claude-code#29966`, filed 2026-03-02, open at last activity 2026-07-29), so a resumed batch re-pays its whole prefix — one measured session wasted ~378,000 uncached tokens.
